p.src: Now Jiang Wei withdrew his army and encamped at Zhongdi, while the Wei forces camped outside the city of Didao. Wang Jing welcomed Chen Tai and Deng Ai into the city, thanked them for lifting the siege, held a banquet in their honor, and richly rewarded the entire army. Chen Tai reported Deng Ai's achievements to Cao Mao, the ruler of Wei. Cao Mao appointed Deng Ai General Who Pacifies the West, granted him imperial authority, and placed him concurrently in command as Colonel Protector of the Eastern Qiang; together with Chen Tai, he was to station troops throughout Yong and Liang. After Deng Ai submitted a memorial thanking the throne, Chen Tai gave a banquet to congratulate him and said, “Jiang Wei fled by night; his strength is spent, and he will not dare come out again.” Deng Ai laughed and said, “By my reckoning, there are five reasons the Shu army is certain to come out again.” Chen Tai asked him why. Deng Ai said, “Though the Shu army has withdrawn, it still possesses the momentum of victory; whereas our army remains weakened by the reality of defeat. That is the first reason they are certain to come. The soldiers of Shu were all drilled under Kongming and are seasoned elite troops, easily maneuvered; our commanders are constantly being replaced, and our troops are not yet thoroughly trained. That is the second reason. The men of Shu mostly travel by boat, while our army must march overland, so their exertion and ours are unequal. That is the third reason. Didao, Longxi, Nan'an, and Qishan are all places that must be defended and contested; the men of Shu may feint east and strike west, or point south and attack north, forcing our troops to divide and guard every quarter; the Shu forces, united in one body, will thus pit their whole strength against each quarter of ours. That is the fourth reason. If the Shu army comes by way of Nan'an or Longxi, it can seize the Qiang people's grain for provisions; if it comes through Qishan, there is wheat upon which it can subsist. That is the fifth reason they are certain to come.” Chen Tai sighed in admiration and said, “You divine the enemy's intentions as if inspired by a god. What is there to fear from the army of Shu?” Thereupon Chen Tai and Deng Ai became close friends despite the difference in their ages. Deng Ai then drilled the troops of Yong, Liang, and the surrounding regions every day; and at every strategic pass he established fortified camps against any unforeseen attack.

p.src: Meanwhile, Jiang Wei held a great banquet at Zhongdi, assembled his generals, and discussed another campaign against Wei. Fan Jian, Clerk of the Secretariat, remonstrated: “General, you have marched out repeatedly without gaining a complete victory. After the recent battle west of the Tao River, the men of Wei already stand in awe of your renown. Why do you wish to march out again? Should the campaign go ill, all your former achievements will be lost.” Jiang Wei said, “You know only that Wei's territory is broad and its population great, and that it cannot be conquered quickly; but you do not know that there are five grounds upon which an attack on Wei can succeed.” The assembled officers asked what they were. Jiang Wei replied, “Their one defeat west of the Tao River utterly broke their keen spirit, whereas our army withdrew without suffering losses. If we advance now, that is our first ground for victory. Our troops will advance by boat and suffer no exhaustion, while theirs must come overland to meet us. That is our second ground for victory. Our soldiers are veterans of long training, whereas theirs are a disorderly rabble without discipline. That is our third ground for victory. Our army can march out through Qishan and seize the autumn grain for provisions. That is our fourth ground for victory. Though their troops guard each place, their strength is divided; if our army advances in one body, how can they reinforce one another? That is our fifth ground for victory. If we do not attack Wei now, what other time shall we await?” Xiahou Ba said, “Though Deng Ai is young, his schemes are deep and far-reaching. He was recently appointed General Who Pacifies the West and is certain to have made preparations everywhere. Matters are no longer as they were before.” Jiang Wei cried sternly, “Why should I fear him? You gentlemen must not magnify another's vigor while diminishing your own might! My mind is made up: I shall take Longxi first.” None dared remonstrate further.

p.src: Jiang Wei personally led the vanguard and ordered the other generals to follow behind. Thus the entire Shu army left Zhongdi and rushed toward Qishan. Scouts reported that the Wei army had already established nine fortified camps at Qishan. Jiang Wei did not believe it. Taking several horsemen, he climbed to high ground and looked out; sure enough, he saw the nine camps of Qishan arrayed like a long serpent, head and tail supporting each other. Jiang Wei turned to those beside him and said, “Xiahou Ba's words were indeed no falsehood. The disposition of these camps is exquisite; only my master, Chancellor Zhuge, could have devised its like. Judging by what Deng Ai has done here, he is no less able than my master.” He returned to his own camp and summoned his generals, saying, “Since the men of Wei have made preparations, they must know that we are coming. I reckon Deng Ai must be here. Display my banners here as a feint, fortify a camp at the mouth of this valley, and send out more than a hundred mounted scouts each day. Each time they ride out on patrol, have them change their armor and clothing. Change the standards in turn among the five directional colors: blue-green, yellow, red, white, and black. Meanwhile, I shall lead the main army secretly out through Dongting and go straight to make a surprise attack on Nan'an.” He then ordered Bao Su to remain at the mouth of the Qishan valley. Jiang Wei led the whole of the main army onward toward Nan'an.

p.src: Meanwhile, when Deng Ai learned that the Shu army had come out through Qishan, he and Chen Tai had already encamped and prepared to meet it; but for several days the Shu forces did not come to challenge them, while mounted scouts rode out from their camp five times a day, going ten or fifteen li before returning. After observing from high ground, Deng Ai hurried into the command tent and said to Chen Tai, “Jiang Wei is not here. He must have gone through Dongting to make a surprise attack on Nan'an. The scouts leaving the camp are merely the same few horsemen, changing their armor and clothing as they ride back and forth on patrol. Their horses are all exhausted, and the commander left here can be no man of ability. General Chen, lead a force against them; their camp can be broken. Once you have smashed their stockade, lead your troops along the road to Dongting and first cut off Jiang Wei's rear. I shall lead another force ahead to relieve Nan'an and go straight to Mount Wucheng. If I seize that summit first, Jiang Wei will certainly make for Shanggui. At Shanggui there is a valley called Duan Valley; its ground is narrow and its mountains steep, making it ideal for an ambush. When he comes to contest Mount Wucheng, I shall first conceal two forces in Duan Valley, and Jiang Wei will surely be defeated.” Chen Tai said, “I have guarded Longxi for twenty or thirty years, yet never have I understood its terrain so clearly. What you have said is truly a godlike calculation. You must go swiftly. I shall attack the stockade here myself.” Thereupon Deng Ai led his army on a forced march through the night and went straight to Mount Wucheng; when his camp was established and the Shu army had not yet arrived, he ordered his son Deng Zhong and Shi Zuan, a colonel of his personal staff, each to lead five thousand men ahead and lie in ambush in Duan Valley, instructing them precisely how to proceed. The two men accepted the plan and departed. Deng Ai ordered the banners furled and the drums silenced as he awaited the Shu army.

p.src: Meanwhile, Jiang Wei came from Dongting toward Nan'an. On reaching the foot of Mount Wucheng, he said to Xiahou Ba, “Near Nan'an there is a mountain called Mount Wucheng. If we seize it first, we can gain the commanding advantage over Nan'an. I fear only that the resourceful Deng Ai will already have taken precautions.” While he was still in doubt, a cannon suddenly boomed from the mountain. Mighty battle cries arose, drums and horns sounded together, and standards sprang up everywhere—all were troops of Wei. In the center, a yellow banner unfurled in the wind, bearing the great characters “Deng Ai.” The Shu soldiers were greatly alarmed. Elite troops charged down from several points on the mountain with irresistible force, and the Shu vanguard was routed. Jiang Wei hastily led the central division to their aid, but by the time he arrived, the Wei troops had already withdrawn. Jiang Wei went straight to the foot of Mount Wucheng and challenged Deng Ai to battle, but the Wei troops on the mountain would not come down. Jiang Wei ordered his soldiers to shout insults. At evening, just as he was about to withdraw, drums and horns sounded together upon the mountain, yet again no Wei troops came down. Jiang Wei tried to storm up the mountain, but the bombardment of stones from above was too fierce for him to advance. He held his position until the third watch, but when he was about to turn back, the drums and horns on the mountain sounded once more. Jiang Wei moved his troops down the mountain and encamped. By the time he had ordered his soldiers to carry timber and stones and was just about to erect the camp defenses, drums and horns sounded again on the mountain, and the Wei troops suddenly swept down. The Shu army fell into utter confusion, trampled one another, and retreated to its former camp.

p.src: The next day, Jiang Wei ordered his soldiers to transport provisions, carts, and equipment to Wucheng Mountain, where they linked and arranged them, intending to erect a stockade and establish a garrison. That night, at the second watch, Deng Ai sent five hundred men down the mountain by two routes, each carrying a torch, to set fire to the carts and equipment. The two armies fought in confusion throughout the night, and the camp could not be completed. Jiang Wei again withdrew his troops and consulted Xiahou Ba: “Since we have not taken Nan'an, we should seize Shanggui first. Shanggui is where Nan'an stores its provisions; if we gain Shanggui, Nan'an will be imperiled of itself.” He therefore left Xiahou Ba to hold Wucheng Mountain. Jiang Wei then led all his elite troops and valiant generals straight toward Shanggui. After marching all night, as dawn approached, he saw that the mountains were narrow and steep and the road rugged. He asked the local guide, “What is this place called?” The guide replied, “Duan Valley.” Jiang Wei was greatly alarmed. “The name is inauspicious: ‘Duan Valley’ sounds like ‘Severed Valley.’ What shall we do if someone cuts off the mouth of the valley?”

p.src: While he hesitated, unable to decide, a sudden report came from the vanguard: “Great clouds of dust are rising behind the mountain. There must be an ambush.” Jiang Wei urgently ordered a retreat, but the two forces of Shi Zuan and Deng Zhong charged out. Jiang Wei fought as he withdrew. Then tremendous battle cries arose ahead, and Deng Ai led his troops into the attack. Assailed from three sides, the Shu army was utterly defeated. Fortunately, Xiahou Ba arrived with his troops and attacked. Only then did the Wei forces withdraw, allowing him to rescue Jiang Wei, who wished to head once more for Mount Qi. Xiahou Ba said, “The stronghold on Mount Qi has already been broken by Chen Tai. Bao Su was killed in battle, and all the men and horses of the camp have withdrawn to Hanzhong.” Jiang Wei dared not go by Dongting and hastily returned along a remote mountain path. Deng Ai pursued close behind. Jiang Wei ordered the various units to press onward while he personally guarded the rear. As they marched, an army suddenly burst from the mountains. It was led by the Wei general Chen Tai. With a single battle cry, the Wei troops surrounded Jiang Wei at their center. Jiang Wei's men and horses were exhausted. They charged left and right but could not break free. Zhang Ni, General Who Sweeps Away Bandits, heard that Jiang Wei was trapped and led several hundred horsemen into the encirclement. Taking advantage of the opening, Jiang Wei fought his way out. Zhang Ni was killed by a storm of arrows from the Wei troops. Having escaped the encirclement, Jiang Wei returned once more to Hanzhong; moved by Zhang Ni's loyalty and valor and his death in the service of the state, he submitted a memorial requesting honors for Zhang Ni's descendants. Many officers and soldiers of Shu had fallen in battle, and all the blame was laid upon Jiang Wei. Following the precedent set by the Martial Marquis after the defeat at Jieting, Jiang Wei submitted a memorial demoting himself to General of the Rear, while continuing to perform the duties of General-in-Chief.

p.src: At this time, Cao Mao, emperor of Wei, changed the third year of Zhengyuan to the first year of Ganlu. Sima Zhao appointed himself Supreme Commander of All Forces Under Heaven. Whenever he went out or came in, three thousand valiant armored warriors always crowded before and behind him as guards; all affairs were decided in his chancellery without being reported to the imperial court. From then on, he constantly harbored thoughts of usurpation and rebellion; he feared only that the people of north and south had not yet submitted in heart. He had a trusted confidant named Jia Chong, courtesy name Gonglü, son of the late General Who Establishes Might, Jia Kui, who served as chief clerk in Sima Zhao's household. Jia Chong said to Sima Zhao, “My lord now holds the supreme power, but the hearts of people throughout the realm are surely not yet settled; we should first sound them out in secret and only then slowly plan the great undertaking.” Sima Zhao replied, “That is precisely what I intend. Travel east on my behalf. Claim merely that you are going to慰問 the soldiers on campaign, and use the opportunity to gather intelligence.” Jia Chong accepted the command and went directly to Huainan, where he called upon Zhuge Dan, Senior General Who Guards the East. Zhuge Dan's courtesy name was Gongxiu. A native of Nanyang in Langya, he was a younger clansman of the Martial Marquis; he had long served Wei, but because the Martial Marquis was chancellor in Shu, he had not been entrusted with important office; after the Martial Marquis died, Zhuge Dan successively held important posts in Wei, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gaoping, and assumed overall command of the forces in the Huai regions. That day, under the pretext of慰問ing the army, Jia Chong arrived in Huainan and met Zhuge Dan. Zhuge Dan held a banquet in his honor. When the wine had taken effect, Jia Chong tested Zhuge Dan with these words: “Recently, the worthy men of Luoyang have all been saying that His Majesty is weak and unfit to rule. For three generations, the Sima family has upheld the state, and its merit and virtue fill the heavens. The General-in-Chief may rightly receive the abdication and succeed to the rule of Wei. I wonder what your honored opinion may be?” Zhuge Dan flew into a rage. “You are the son of Governor Jia of Yuzhou, and your family has lived for generations on the stipends of Wei. How dare you utter such seditious words!” Jia Chong apologized. “I was merely relating what others have said.” Zhuge Dan said, “Should the imperial court face danger, I shall repay it with my life.” Jia Chong fell silent.

p.src: At this time, Sun Jun, chancellor of Eastern Wu, died of illness, and his younger cousin Sun Chen took charge of the government. Sun Chen's courtesy name was Zitong. Violent and tyrannical by nature, he killed Grand Marshal Teng Yin, General Lü Ju, Wang Dun, and others; thus all power fell into his hands. Though Sun Liang, ruler of Wu, was intelligent, there was nothing he could do. Wu Gang therefore brought Zhuge Jing to Stone City and went in to pay his respects to Sun Chen. Sun Chen asked why they had come. Wu Gang replied, “Zhuge Dan is a younger clansman of Zhuge, the Martial Marquis of Shu-Han, and has long served the state of Wei; now, seeing Sima Zhao deceive the sovereign and defy his superiors, depose rulers, and abuse his power, he wishes to raise an army against him. But his strength is insufficient, and so he has come especially to submit to Wu. Fearing that his sincerity might lack proof, he has expressly sent his own son Zhuge Jing as a hostage. We humbly beg you to send troops to his aid.” Sun Chen granted the request. He appointed the senior generals Quan Yi and Quan Duan as chief commanders, Yu Quan to guard the rear, Zhu Yi and Tang Zi as vanguard commanders, and Wen Qin as guide. He raised seventy thousand troops and advanced in three divisions. Wu Gang returned to Shouchun and reported the news to Zhuge Dan. Zhuge Dan was overjoyed and deployed his troops in readiness.

p.src: Now Zhuge Dan's memorial reached Luoyang. When Sima Zhao read it, he flew into a rage and wished to march against him in person. Jia Chong remonstrated: “My lord, you have inherited the foundations laid by your father and elder brother, yet your benevolence has not reached all under Heaven. If you now leave the Son of Heaven behind and depart, and some upheaval should suddenly occur, it will be too late for regret. It would be better to petition the Empress Dowager and the Son of Heaven to accompany the expedition; then there will be nothing to fear.” Sima Zhao said with delight, “Those words accord perfectly with my own thoughts.” He therefore entered the palace and memorialized the Empress Dowager: “Zhuge Dan has rebelled. I have assembled the civil and military officials, and our deliberations are complete. I ask that Your Majesty accompany the Son of Heaven on an imperial expedition, thereby carrying on the late emperor's final purpose.” The Empress Dowager was afraid and had no choice but to comply. The next day, Sima Zhao asked Cao Mao, ruler of Wei, to set out. Cao Mao said, “As General-in-Chief, you command all the armies of the realm and may deploy them as you please. Why must I go in person?” Sima Zhao replied, “That is not so. In former days, the Martial Founder ranged victorious throughout the realm; Emperor Wen and Emperor Ming aspired to embrace the whole universe and bring all the farthest lands under their sway. Whenever they encountered a formidable enemy, they invariably went in person. Your Majesty should follow worthily in the footsteps of your forebears and sweep away this old miscreant. Why should you be afraid?” Overawed by Sima Zhao's power, Cao Mao had no choice but to comply. Before three bouts had passed, Zhu Yi was defeated and fled; Tang Zi then rode out, but he too was soundly defeated and fled before three bouts were over. Wang Ji drove his troops forward in pursuit and slaughter. The Wu army suffered a crushing defeat, withdrew fifty li, and made camp; news of the reverse was carried into Shouchun. Zhuge Dan personally led the picked troops under his own command and joined forces with Wen Qin and his two sons, Wen Yang and Wen Hu.
